shack.e: Unknown. Some scholars derive this word from Mexican Spanish jacal, from Nahuatl xacalli (“adobe hut”). Alternatively, the word may instead come from ramshackle/ramshackly (e.g., old ramshackly house) or perhaps it may be a back-formation from shackly.
shack.g: A crude, roughly built hut or cabin.
Grain fallen to the ground and left after harvest.

shackle.e: From Middle English shakel, schakkyl, schakle (“a fetter, shackle; coupling used to connect a plough or wagon to a draft chain”), from Old English sċacul, sċeacel, sċeacul (“fetter, shackle”), from Proto-West Germanic *skakul, from Proto-Germanic *skakulaz (“shackle”), possibly from *skakaną (“to shake; to swing; to escape”).
shackle.g: A restraint fitted over a human or animal appendage, such as an ankle, finger, or wrist, normally used in a pair joined by a chain.

shackle.e: From Middle English schakelen, schakkylen (“(also figurative) to put (someone) in shackles; to protect (legs) with greaves”), from shakel, schakkyl, schakle (noun) (see etymology 1) + -en (suffix forming the infinitives of verbs).
shackle.g: To place (a person or animal) in shackles (noun etymology 1 sense 1); to immobilize or restrain using shackles.

shade.e: From Middle English schade, from Old English sċeadu, from Proto-West Germanic *skadu, from Proto-Germanic *skaduz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ḱh₃tús, from *(s)ḱeh₃-.
shade.g: Darkness where light, particularly sunlight, is blocked.

shade.e: From Middle English schaden, from schade + -en.
shade.g: To shield (someone or something) from light.

shadow.e: From Middle English schadowe, schadewe, schadwe (also schade > shade), from Old English sċeaduwe, sċeadwe, oblique form of sċeadu (“shadow, shade; darkness; protection”), from Proto-West Germanic *skadu, from Proto-Germanic *skaduz (“shade, shadow”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ḱeh₃- (“darkness”).
shadow.g: A dark image projected onto a surface where light (or other radiation) is blocked by the shade of an object.

shadow.e: From Middle English schadowen, from Old English sċeadwian, from sċeadu (“shadow; shade”) + -ian (suffix forming verbs).

shadowing.e: From shadow (verb) + -ing (suffix forming nouns denoting the act of doing something, an action, or the embodiment of an action; or forming present participles of verbs).
shadowing.g: The effect of being shadowed (in the sense of blocked), as from a light source or radio transmission.

shaft.e: From Middle English chafte, saft, scaft, schaft, schafte, scheft, shaffet, shaft, from Old English sċeaft, from Proto-West Germanic *skaft, from Proto-Germanic *skaftaz (“shaft”), from Proto-Indo-European *skeh₂p- (“club, rod, shaft, staff”).
shaft.g: The entire body of a long weapon, such as an arrow.

shake.e: From Middle English schaken, from Old English sċeacan, sċacan (“to shake”), from Proto-West Germanic *skakan, from Proto-Germanic *skakaną (“to shake, swing, escape”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)keg-, *(s)kek- (“to jump, move”).
shake.g: To cause (something) to move rapidly in opposite directions alternatingly.

shaken.e: By surface analysis, shake (verb) + -n (a variant of -en (suffix forming past participle forms of verbs; and adjectives)).
shaken.g: Moved rapidly in opposite directions alternatingly.

shall.e: From Middle English schal (infinitive schulen), from Old English sċeal (infinitive sċulan (“should, must”)), from Proto-West Germanic *skulan, from Proto-Germanic *skal (infinitive *skulaną), from Proto-Indo-European *skel- (“to owe, be under obligation”).
shall.g: Used before a verb to indicate the simple future tense in the first person singular or plural.

shallow.e: From Middle English schalowe (“not deep, shallow”); apparently related to Middle English schalde, schold, scheld, schealde (“shallow”), from Old English sċeald (“shallow”), from Proto-Germanic *skal-, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelh₁- (“to parch, dry out”).
shallow.g: Having little depth; significantly less deep than wide.

shalom.e: Borrowed from Hebrew שָׁלוֹם (šālóm, “peace, well-being; Hello, good-bye”).
shalom.g: A traditional Jewish greeting or farewell.

shambles.e: From Middle English schamels, plural of schamel, from Old English sċeamol, sċamul (“bench, stool”), from Proto-West Germanic *skamul, *skamil (“stool, bench”), from Vulgar Latin scamellum, from Latin scamillum (“little bench, ridge”), from Latin scamnum (“bench, ridge, breadth of a field”).
shambles.g: A scene of great disorder or ruin.

shame.e: From Middle English schame, from Old English sċamu, from Proto-West Germanic *skamu, from Proto-Germanic *skamō.
shame.g: An uncomfortable or painful feeling due to recognition or consciousness of one's own impropriety or dishonor, or something being exposed tha

shame.e: From Middle English schamen, from Old English sċamian, from Proto-West Germanic *skamēn, from Proto-Germanic *skamāną.

shamefacedness.e: From an alteration of Middle English schamefastnesse, equivalent to shamefaced + -ness.

shameful.e: From Middle English schameful, schamfull, from Old English *sċeamfull, sċeomfull, equivalent to shame + -ful.
shameful.g: Causing or meriting shame or disgrace; disgraceful

shamefully.e: From Middle English schamefully. By surface analysis, shameful + -ly.

shameless.e: From Middle English schameles, shameles, from Old English sċamlēas, sċeamlēas (“without shame; shameless”), from Proto-Germanic *skamalausaz (“shameless”), equivalent to shame + -less.
shameless.g: Having no shame, no guilt nor remorse over something considered wrong; immodest, brazen; unable to feel disgrace.

shan.e: Origin obscure. Perhaps from shand (“worthless”). Alternatively, perhaps of Romani origin.

shape.e: From Middle English schap, schape, from Old English ġesceap (“shape, form, created being, creature, creation, dispensation, fate, condition, sex, gender, genitalia”), from Proto-West Germanic *ga- + *skap, from Proto-Germanic *ga- + *skapą (“shape, nature, condition”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kep- (“to split, cut”).
shape.g: The status or condition of something

shaped.e: From Middle English schaped, ischaped, equivalent to shape + -ed.
shaped.g: Having been given a shape, especially a curved shape.

shapely.e: From Middle English schaply, schappely (“well-shaped, beautiful, attractive”), perhaps from Old English *ġesċeaplīċ (“according to design, proper, fit”) (suggested by Old English ġesċeaplīċe (“properly, fitting, well”)), equivalent to shape + -ly.
shapely.g: Having a pleasing shape, pleasant to look at.

shapen.e: From Middle English schapen, ischepen, from Old English ġesċapen, from Proto-Germanic *skapanaz, past participle of Proto-Germanic *skapaną, equivalent to shape + -en (past participle ending).
shapen.g: Shaped; wrought with a definite shape.

shaping.e: From Middle English shapinge, shapende, schapende, schappande, from Old English sċyppende, sċeppende, from Proto-West Germanic *skappjandī, from Proto-Germanic *skapjandz, present participle of Proto-Germanic *skapjaną (“to form, shape, create”), equivalent to shape + -ing.

shard.e: From Middle English shard, scherd, scheard, schord, from Old English sċeard (“a broken piece; shard”), from Proto-West Germanic *skard, from Proto-Germanic *skardą (“notch; nick”), from *skardaz (“damaged; nicked; scarred”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut”).
shard.g: A piece of broken glass or pottery, especially one found in an archaeological dig.

share.e: From Middle English schare, schere, from Old English sċearu (“a cutting, shaving, a shearing, tonsure, part, division, share”), from Proto-West Germanic *skaru, from Proto-Germanic *skarō (“a division, detachment”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut, divide”).
share.g: A portion of something, especially a portion given or allotted to someone.

share.e: From Middle English schar, schare, from Old English sċear, sċær (“ploughshare”), from Proto-Germanic *skaraz (“ploughshare”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut”).
share.g: The cutting blade of an agricultural machine like a plough, a cultivator or a seeding-machine.

sharp.e: From Middle English scharp, from Old English sċearp, from Proto-West Germanic *skarp, from Proto-Germanic *skarpaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerb-, from *(s)ker- (“to cut”).
sharp.g: Terminating in a point or edge, especially one that can cut or pierce easily; not dull, obtuse, or rounded.

sharpen.e: From Middle English scharpenen, scharpnen, equivalent to sharp + -en.

sharper.g: A swindler; a cheat; a professional gambler who makes his living by cheating.

sharply.e: From Middle English sharply, scharply, from Old English sċearplīċe (“sharply, smartly”), equivalent to sharp + -ly.
sharply.g: In a sharp manner, in various senses.

sharpness.e: From Middle English sharpnesse, scharpnesse, from Old English sċearpnes (“sharpness”), equivalent to sharp + -ness.
sharpness.g: the cutting ability of an edge; keenness.

shatter.e: From Middle English schateren (“to scatter, dash”), an assibilated form of Middle English scateren ("to scatter"; see scatter), from Old English scaterian, from Proto-Germanic *skat- (“to smash, scatter”), perhaps ultimately imitative.
shatter.g: Of brittle solid materials (like glass or ice), to violently break into pieces.

shave.e: From Middle English shaven, schaven, from Old English sċafan (“to shave, scrape, shred, polish”), from Proto-West Germanic *skaban, from Proto-Germanic *skabaną (“to scrape”), from Proto-Indo-European *skabʰ- (“to cut, split, form, carve”).
shave.g: To make (the head, skin etc.) bald or (the hair) shorter by using a tool such as a razor or electric clippers to cut the hair close to the s

shave.e: From Middle English shave, from Old English sceafa, from Proto-Germanic *skabô.

shawl.e: Borrowed from Hindustani (Hindi शाल (śāl) / Urdu شال (śāl)), from Classical Persian شال (šāl).
shawl.g: A square or rectangular piece of cloth worn as a covering for the head, neck, and shoulders, typically by women.

sheaf.e: From Middle English scheef, from Old English sċēaf, from Proto-West Germanic *skaub, from Proto-Germanic *skauba- (“sheaf”).
sheaf.g: A quantity of the stalks and ears of wheat, rye, or other grain, bound together; a bundle of grain or straw.

shear.e: From Middle English sheren, scheren, from Old English sċieran (“to shear; to shave”), from Proto-West Germanic *skeran, from Proto-Germanic *skeraną, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut”).
shear.g: To remove the fleece from (a sheep, llama, etc.) by clipping.

shearing.e: From Middle English scherynge; equivalent to shear + -ing.

sheath.e: From Middle English sheth, shethe (“holder for a sword, knife, etc., scabbard, sheath”), from Old English sċēaþ (“sheath”), from Proto-West Germanic *skaiþiju, from Proto-Germanic *skaiþiz (“sheath; covering”), from Proto-Indo-European *skey- (“to dissect, split”) (possibly from the notion of a split stick with a sword inserted).
sheath.g: A holster for a sword; a scabbard.

sheave.e: From Middle English, from a Germanic base akin to German Scheibe, late Old Norse skífa (“slice”), all ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *skey- (“to split”). For more see shive.
sheave.g: A wheel having a groove in the rim for a rope to work in, and set in a block, mast, or similar; the wheel of a pulley.

shed.e: From Middle English scheden, schede, from Old English scēadan, scādan (“to separate, divide, part, make a line of separation between; remove from association or companionship; distinguish, discriminate, decide, determine, appoint; shatter, shed; expound; decree; write down; differ”), from Proto-West Germanic *skaiþan.
From Middle English sched, schede, schad, from a combination of Old English scēada (“a parting of the hair, top of the head”) and Old English ġesċēad (“distinction, reason”).
shed.g: An opening between upper and lower warp yarns through which the weft is woven.

sheep.e: From Middle English schep, schepe, from Anglian Old English sċēp (West Saxon sċēap), from Proto-West Germanic *skāp, from Proto-Germanic *skēpą, of unknown origin.
sheep.g: A woolly ruminant of the genus Ovis.

sheepcote.g: A small building for sheltering sheep.

sheepfold.e: From Middle English shepefald, perhaps from Late Old English sċēapa falde (literally “sheep's fold”), equivalent to sheep + fold.

sheepherder.g: A person who herds sheep; a shepherd.

sheepskin.g: The skin of a sheep, especially an adult sheep, and especially when used to make parchment or in bookbinding.

sheer.e: From Middle English shere, scheere, schere, skere, from Old English sċǣre (“pure, sheer; shining, clear”), from Proto-Germanic *skairiz; supplanted the semantically close shire (dialectal), from Middle English schyre, schire, shire, shir, from Old English sċīr (“clear, bright; brilliant, gleaming, shining, splendid, resplendent.
Perhaps from Dutch scheren (“to move aside, skim”); see also shear.
sheer.g: The curve of the main deck or gunwale from bow to stern.

shekel.e: From Hebrew שֶׁקֶל (shékel, “shekel”), from שָׁקַל (shakál, “to weigh”), from Akkadian 𒂅 (šiqlum).
shekel.g: A currency unit of both ancient and modern Israel.

shelter.e: From Middle English sheltron, sheldtrume (“roof or wall formed by locked shields”), from Old English sċildtruma, sċyldtruma (“a phalanx, company (of troops), a tortoise, a covering, shed, shelter”, literally “shield-troop”), from sċyld, sċield (“shield”) + truma (“a troop of soldiers”).

shepherd.e: From Middle English schepherde, from Old English sċēaphierde, a compound of sċēap (“sheep”) and hierde (“herdsman”), equivalent to modern sheep + herd (“herder”).
shepherd.g: A person who tends sheep, especially a grazing flock.

shepherdess.e: From Middle English scheperdesse, shepperdesse; equivalent to shepherd + -ess.

sheriff.e: From Middle English shirreve, in turn inherited from Old English sċīrġerēfa, corresponding to shire + reeve. There is no etymological connection to sharif (Arabic شَرِيف (šarīf)), an Arabic title of honour with cognates in other languages, including Persian, Punjabi, Bengali, Hindi, Urdu, Turkish, Spanish, Portuguese, etc.
sheriff.g: (High Sheriff) An official of a shire or county office, responsible for carrying out court orders, law enforcement and other duties.

sheweth.e: shew + -eth, the archaic third-person singular present tense suffix.

shield.e: From Middle English scheld, shelde, from Old English scield (“shield”), from Proto-West Germanic *skeldu, from Proto-Germanic *skelduz (“shield”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelH- (“cut, split”).
shield.g: Anything that protects or defends; defense; shelter; protection.

shield.e: An alteration of Middle English schilden after Etymology 1, from Old English sċildan, from Proto-West Germanic *skildijan, form Proto-Germanic *skildijaną.

shield-bearer.e: From Middle English scheeld-berere, equivalent to shield + bearer.
shield-bearer.g: A person who carries a shield, either a warrior, or a lower-ranking person who carries a shield for a higher-ranking person.

shimmer.e: From Middle English schimeren, from Old English sċymrian, sċimrian, sċimerian, from Proto-Germanic *skimarōną.
shimmer.g: To shine tremulously or intermittently; to gleam faintly.

shine.e: From Middle English shinen, schinen (preterite schon, past participle schinen), from Old English sċīnan (“to shine, flash; be resplendent”; preterite sċān, past participle sċinen), from Proto-West Germanic *skīnan (“to shine”), from Proto-Germanic *skīnaną (“to shine”).
shine.g: To emit or reflect light so as to glow.

shine.e: From the noun shine, or perhaps continuing Middle English schinen in its causative uses, from Old English scīn (“brightness, shine”), and also Middle English schenen, from Old English scǣnan (“to render brilliant, make shine”), from Proto-Germanic *skainijaną, causative of *skīnaną (“to shine”).
shine.g: To cause (something) to be smooth and shiny by rubbing; put a shine on (something); polish (something).

ship.e: From Middle English chip, schepe, schip, schup, scip, scippe, ship, shup, ssip, from Old English sċip, sċyp, from Proto-West Germanic *skip, from Proto-Germanic *skipą (“ship; tub, vessel”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *skey- (“to split”).
ship.g: A water-borne vessel generally larger than a boat.

ship.e: From Middle English schippen, schipen, from Old English sċipian, from Proto-West Germanic *skipōn, from Proto-Germanic *skipōną, from Proto-Germanic *skipą (“ship”).

shipmaster.e: From Middle English schypmayster, schypmester, equivalent to ship + master.
shipmaster.g: The master of a ship; a captain; a commander.

shipwreck.e: From Middle English schipwrak, from Old English sċipwræc (“jetsam”), equivalent to ship + wrack. Modern form is due to influence from wreck. By surface analysis, ship + wreck.
shipwreck.g: A ship that has sunk or run aground so that it is no longer seaworthy; a ruined vessel or its remains.

shipwright.e: From Middle English shipwright, shippwright, schipwricht, ship-wriȝth, from Old English sċipwyrhta, equivalent to ship + wright (“builder”).
shipwright.g: A person who designs, builds and repairs ships, especially wooden ones.

shittah.e: Borrowed from Hebrew שִׁטָּה (shitá), usually expressed in its plural form שִׁטִּים (shitím).
shittah.g: A tree said in the Bible to have furnished the precious wood of which the ark, tables, altars, boards, etc., of the Jewish tabernacle were m

shiver.e: Origin uncertain, perhaps an alteration of chavel, or a frequentive of sheaf.
shiver.g: To tremble or shake, especially when cold or frightened.

shiver.e: From a Germanic word, probably present in Old English though unattested, cognate with Old High German scivaro (German Schiefer (“slate”)).
shiver.g: A fragment or splinter, especially of glass or stone.

shock.e: From Middle Dutch schokken (“to push, jolt, shake, jerk”) or Middle French choquer (“to collide with, clash”), from Old Dutch *skokkan (“to shake up and down, shog”), from Proto-Germanic *skukkaną (“to move, shake, tremble”). Of uncertain origin. Perhaps related to Proto-Germanic *skakaną (“to shake, stir”).
From Middle English schok, from Old English *sċoc or Middle Low German schok; in any case, from Proto-West Germanic *skok and possibly related to Latvian kàudze and Lithuanian kiūgis.
shock.g: An arrangement of sheaves for drying; a stook.

shod.e: From Middle English shoed, past participle of shon.

shoe.e: From Middle English scho, sho, from Old English sċōh (“shoe”), from Proto-West Germanic *skōh, from Proto-Germanic *skōhaz (“shoe”), of unclear etymology; possibly a derivation from *skehaną (“to move quickly”), from Proto-Indo-European *skek- (“to move quickly, jump”).
shoe.g: A protective covering for the foot, with a bottom part composed of thick leather or plastic sole and often a thicker heel, and a softer uppe

shoot.e: From Middle English scheten, schoten, from Old English scēotan, from Proto-West Germanic *skeutan, from Proto-Germanic *skeutaną, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kéwd-e-ti, thematic present of *(s)kewd- (“to shoot, throw”).
shoot.g: To launch (forcefully project) (a projectile or similar object).
A mild expletive, expressing disbelief or dismay

shooter.e: From Middle English schoter, schuter, schotter, scheter, schetare, scheotere, from Old English sċēotere (“shooter”), equivalent to shoot + -er.
shooter.g: Someone who shoots something; a gunner, archer, etc.

shooting.e: From Middle English shoting, schoting, from Old English scotung (“shooting”), from Proto-Germanic *skutungō, equivalent to shoot + -ing.

shore.e: From Middle English schore, from Old English *sċora (attested as sċor- in placenames), from Proto-Germanic *skurô (“rugged rock, cliff, high rocky shore”). Possibly related to Old English sċieran (“to cut”), which survives today as English shear. Maybe connected with Norwegian Bokmål skjær.
shore.g: Land adjoining a non-flowing body of water, such as an ocean, lake or pond.

shore.e: Uncertain. The word is attested in Northern English and Scots; the DSL states that schore "to threaten" is attested before 1400 (a corresponding noun schoyr is attested since 1375: "vith gret schoyr and mannasyng" in Barbour's Bruce), and suggests it might ultimately be related to Old Scots schoir "steep (of a crag)", related to shear.
shore.g: To threaten or warn unpleasant consequences (for someone); (sometimes) to threaten or warn off or scare away.

short.e: From Middle English schort, short, from Old English sċeort, sċort (“short”), from Proto-West Germanic *skurt, from Proto-Germanic *skurtaz (“short”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker-.
short.g: Having a small distance from one end or edge to another, either horizontally or vertically.

shortcoming.g: A deficiency or falling short; failure to attain a goal or ideal.

shorten.e: From Middle English shortnen, schortenen, equivalent to short + -en (verbal suffix). In some senses, a continuation (in altered form) of Middle English schorten (“to make short, shorten”), from Old English sċortian (“to become short”), from Proto-Germanic *skurtōną (“to shorten”).

shortfall.e: Deverbal from fall short. By surface analysis, short + fall.
shortfall.g: An instance of falling short, of not meeting a quota, an obligation, or more generally any expected target.

shortly.e: From Middle English schortly, schortliche, from Old English sċortlīċe (“shortly; before long; soon”), equivalent to short + -ly.
shortly.g: In a short or brief time or manner; quickly.

shoulder.e: From Middle English schuldre, sholder, shulder, schulder, from Old English sċuldra, sċuldor (“shoulder”), from Proto-West Germanic *skuldru (“shoulder”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps related to Proto-Germanic *skelduz (“shield”), see shield.
shoulder.g: The part of an animal's body between the base of the neck and arm socket.

shout.e: From Middle English shouten. Further origin uncertain. Possibly related to Middle English shooten (“to shoot (out)”) or from or akin to Old Norse skúta (“to chide, scold”), Old Norse skúti, skúta (“a taunt”).
shout.g: A loud burst of voice or voices; a violent and sudden outcry, especially that of a multitude expressing joy, triumph, exultation, anger, or

shout.e: From Middle English shout(e), from Middle Dutch schûte (“boat or light ship”).
shout.g: A flat-bottomed boat, a barge (for carrying cargo, etc), now especially a light boat used in duck-shooting.

shove.e: From Middle English schouven, from Old English sċūfan, from Proto-West Germanic *skeuban, from Proto-Germanic *skeubaną, from Proto-Indo-European *skewbʰ-.
shove.g: To push, especially roughly or with force.

shovel.e: From Middle English schovele, schovel, showell, shole (> English dialectal shoul, shool), from Old English scofl (“shovel”), from Proto-Germanic *skuflō, *skūflō (“shovel”), equivalent to shove + -el (instrumental/agent suffix).
shovel.g: A hand tool with a handle, used for moving portions of material such as earth, snow, and grain from one place to another, with some forms al

show.e: From Middle English schewen, from Old English scēawian (“to look, look at, exhibit, display”), from Proto-West Germanic *skauwōn, from Proto-Germanic *skawwōną (“to look, see”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewh₁- (“to heed, look, feel, take note of”); see haw, gaum, caveat, caution.
show.g: To display, convey or exhibit; to have something available for others to see; to direct attention to something.

show.e: From Middle English schewe, from the verb (schewen).
show.g: A play, dance, or other entertainment.

shower.e: From Middle English schour (“shower”), from Old English sċūr (“shower”), from Proto-West Germanic *skūru (“shower”), from Proto-Germanic *skūrō (“storm, short shower”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ḱēwer- (“north, north wind, cold wind, rain shower”).
shower.g: A brief fall of precipitation (spell of rain, or a similar fall of snow, sleet, or cascade); burst of hefty precipitation.

shower.e: From Middle English schewere, schewer, shewere (“one who exhibits something, actor; watchman; sign; mirror; index finger”), from Old English sċēawere (“an observer, one who examines into a matter; a spy; mirror; actor, buffoon”), equivalent to show + -er.

showing.e: From Middle English schewynge, schewand, schewande, schewende, from Old English sċēawiende, from Proto-West Germanic *skauwōndī, from Proto-Germanic *skawwōndz, present participle of Proto-Germanic *skawwōną (“to look, observe”), equivalent to show + -ing.

shrank.e: From Pennsylvania German; cognate to German Schrank.
shrank.g: A large highly decorative German/Dutch-style piece of furniture, which combines aspects of a clothing wardrobe, curio, and cabinet.

shred.e: From Middle English shrede, shred (“fragment, piece, scrap; piece cut off from something; strip of material; ornamental strip hanging from the edge of a garment; thread; band or thread woven in a garment; element, streak; plant (?)”), from Late Old English sċrēad, sċrēade (“piece cut off from something; a paring; a shred”).
shred.g: A fragment of something; a particle; a piece; also, a very small amount.

shrewd.e: From Middle English schrewed (“depraved; wicked”, literally “accursed”), from schrewen (“to curse; beshrew”), from schrewe, schrowe, screwe (“evil or wicked person/thing”), from Old English sċrēawa (“wicked person”, literally “biter”). Equivalent to shrew + -ed.
shrewd.g: Showing clever resourcefulness in practical matters.

shrewdly.e: From Middle English schrewedly (“wickedly, harshly”). By surface analysis, shrewd + -ly.

shriek.e: From obsolete shrick (1567), shreke, variants of earlier screak, skricke (before 1500), from Middle English scrycke, from a North Germanic/Scandinavian language (compare Swedish skrika, Danish skrige, Icelandic skríkja), from Proto-Germanic *skrīkijaną, *skrik- (compare English screech).
shriek.g: A sharp, shrill outcry or scream; a shrill wild cry caused by sudden or extreme terror, pain, or the like.

shrine.e: From Middle English shryne, from Old English scrīn (“reliquary, ark of the covenant”), from Medieval Latin scrīnium (“reliquary”), “case or chest for books or papers” in Classical Latin. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to turn, bend”).
shrine.g: A holy or sacred place dedicated to a specific deity, ancestor, hero, martyr, saint, or similar figure of awe and respect, at which said fig

shrink.e: From Middle English schrynken, from Old English sċrincan, from Proto-Germanic *skrinkwaną. The sense “psychologist, psychotherapist” is a clipping of head-shrinker.

shrivel.e: First recorded as shriveled (“shrivelled”), probably of North Germanic origin related to dialectal Swedish skryvla (“to wrinkle, shrivel”); perhaps ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *skrinkwaną (“to shrivel, shrink”) or *skrimpaną (“to shrink”).

shroud.e: From Middle English shroud, from Old English sċrūd, from Proto-Germanic *skrūdą (“shroud, dress, attire”).
shroud.g: That which clothes, covers, conceals, or protects; a garment.

shroud.e: From Middle English schrouden (> Anglo-Latin scrudāre), from Middle English schroud (“shroud”) (see above).

shrouded.e: From Middle English schrouded, equivalent to shroud + -ed.
shrouded.g: Wearing, or provided with a shroud.

shrub.e: From Middle English schrub, schrob, (also unassibilated as scrub), from Old English *sċrob (in placenames) and sċrybb (“a shrub; shrubbery; underbrush”); akin to Norwegian skrubbe (“the dwarf cornel tree”).
shrub.g: A woody plant smaller than a tree, and usually with several stems from the same base.

shrub.e: From Arabic شِرَاب (širāb, “a drink, beverage”), شَرِبَ (šariba, “to drink”), akin to syrup, sherbet, and sorbet.
shrub.g: A liquor composed of vegetable acid, fruit juice (especially lemon), sugar, sometimes vinegar, and a small amount of spirit as a preservativ

shudder.e: From Middle English schoderen, schuderen, possibly from Middle Dutch schudderen and/or Middle Low German schodderen, iterative forms of the verb at hand in Dutch schudden, Low German schüdden (both “to shake”), German schütten (“to pour”), from Proto-West Germanic *skuddjan, from Proto-Germanic *skudjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *skewdʰ-.
shudder.g: To shake nervously, often from fear or horror.

shun.e: From Middle English schonen (“to decline to do, avoid, fear”), from Old English sċunian (“to shun, fear, avoid”), of uncertain origin, though probably ultimately connected to the Proto-Indo-European root *(s)kewH- (“to cover, conceal”) via Proto-Germanic *skunōną; see that entry for more discussion.

shut.e: From Middle English schitten, schetten, from Old English sċyttan (“to cause rapid movement, shoot a bolt, shut, bolt”), from Proto-West Germanic *skuttjan, from Proto-Germanic *skutjaną, *skuttijaną (“to bar, bolt”), from Proto-Germanic *skuttą, *skuttjō (“bar, bolt, shed”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewd- (“to drive, fall upon, rush”).
shut.g: Closed, not open, in any of various senses.

shuttle.e: From a merger of two words: Middle English shutel, shotel, schetel, schettell, schyttyl, scutel (“bar; bolt”), from Old English sċyttel, sċutel (“bar; bolt”), equivalent to shut + -le Middle English shutel, schetil, shotil, shetel, schootyll, shutyll, schytle, scytyl (“missile; projectile; spear”), from Old English sċytel, sċutel (“dart, arrow”).
shuttle.g: A tool used to carry the woof back and forth between the warp threads on a loom.

shy.e: From Middle English shy (“shy”), from Old English sċēoh (“shy”), from Proto-West Germanic *skeuh (“shy, fearful”), from Proto-Germanic *skeuhaz (“shy, fearful”).
